lead: A biosensor must pick one molecule out of a blood sample full of others, and the bio-recognition element does that picking. Enzymes catalyse one substrate, antibodies bind one antigen, nucleic acid probes pair with one complementary sequence. The element's kinetics or binding constant sets the sensor's range and detection limit. Glucometer strips, pregnancy tests and DNA test cards all rest on this layer. This chapter covers the three families, the numbers that describe them, and how they are fixed to a transducer.
prereq: You need: 4.1 for the component chain.

blocks.text: Most enzymes are protein catalysts; a few are RNA. It binds one substrate at its active site, converts it, and is released unchanged, so one molecule cycles many times. Activity is quoted in international units: 1 U = 1 µmol of substrate converted per minute. Glucose oxidase, used on every glucose strip, oxidises β-D-glucose and is nearly blind to other sugars.

blocks.where: v is the rate (µmol min⁻¹ per mg of enzyme); V<sub>max</sub> is the rate when every site is occupied; S is substrate concentration; K<sub>m</sub> is the substrate concentration giving v = V<sub>max</sub>/2.

blocks.text: K<sub>m</sub> measures how tightly the enzyme holds its substrate: a small K<sub>m</sub> means tight binding and early saturation. At S = 19 K<sub>m</sub>, v = 0.95 V<sub>max</sub>; above that, doubling S barely changes v, so the sensor cannot resolve two high concentrations. Well below K<sub>m</sub> the rate is nearly proportional to S, v ≈ (V<sub>max</sub>/K<sub>m</sub>) S, and that straight part is the useful range. Glucose oxidase in solution has a K<sub>m</sub> for glucose reported in the region of 20–40 mmol/L, above most blood glucose values. On an electrode the enzyme is immobilised, substrate must diffuse through the layer, and the apparent K<sub>m</sub> usually rises; a diffusion-limiting membrane is often added on purpose to stretch the straight part.

On a glucose electrode the enzyme reaction runs to completion by itself. The electrode oxidises the product, hydrogen peroxide or a reduced mediator, to turn each enzyme turnover into electrons that can be counted as a current.

sections.h3: Antibodies and nucleic acids: binding sets selectivity

blocks.text: An antibody is not a catalyst. It binds an antigen and stays bound; it is neither consumed nor turned over. Affinity is described by the dissociation constant Kd = [antibody][antigen]/[complex]; smaller Kd means tighter binding. A whole IgG has two sites, so multivalent avidity can be far stronger than one site's Kd suggests. Detection is label-free when binding itself changes mass or charge on the transducer, and labelled when a fluorescent or enzyme tag reports the event.

blocks.where: θ is the fraction of antibody sites occupied; [Ag] is the free antigen concentration; K<sub>d</sub> is the dissociation constant, in the same units. At [Ag] = K<sub>d</sub>, half the sites are filled.

blocks.text: A nucleic acid probe is a short single strand, for example a 20-base oligomer. It finds its target by Watson–Crick pairing: A with T, G with C. Hybridisation strengthens as G+C content rises (three hydrogen bonds per G–C pair against two for A–T) and as salt concentration rises, which shields the negative phosphate backbones; it weakens as temperature rises. The melting temperature Tm is where half the duplexes have separated. Whole cells or tissue slices can also be the recognition layer: their own receptors and enzymes respond to the analyte, as in whole-cell sensors for toxicity or biochemical oxygen demand.

Immobilisation methods: adsorption is simple but leaks; covalent coupling is stable; gel entrapment holds whole cells and enzymes; self-assembled monolayers of thiols on gold give an ordered, reproducible surface.

figure.caption: Michaelis–Menten curves for the worked example: V<sub>max</sub> = 120, K<sub>m</sub> = 25 mmol/L in solution and an apparent K<sub>m</sub> of 60 mmol/L on the electrode. Each curve reaches half of V<sub>max</sub> at its own K<sub>m</sub>; the larger apparent K<sub>m</sub> keeps the response closer to a straight line over the blood range.

spec.aria: Two saturating curves of rate against glucose from 0 to 100 mmol/L, one reaching half of 120 at 25 and one at 60 mmol/L, with the 2 to 20 mmol/L blood range shaded and points at 20 mmol/L giving 53.3 and 30.0.

examples.question: A glucose oxidase layer has V<sub>max</sub> = 120 µmol min⁻¹ mg⁻¹ and, in solution, K<sub>m</sub> = 25 mmol/L (a value inside the reported range). (a) Find v at S = 5.0 mmol/L. (b) Show that S = 25 mmol/L gives half of V<sub>max</sub>. (c) Find the concentration giving 95 % of V<sub>max</sub>. (d) At S = 20 mmol/L, compare the actual rate with the straight-line rate (V<sub>max</sub>/K<sub>m</sub>) S, first for K<sub>m</sub> = 25 mmol/L and then for an immobilised layer with apparent K<sub>m</sub> = 60 mmol/L.
steps: Write Michaelis–Menten: v = V<sub>max</sub> S / (K<sub>m</sub> + S).
(b) v = 120 × 25 / (25 + 25) = 3000 / 50 = 60.0 µmol min⁻¹ mg⁻¹, exactly V<sub>max</sub>/2, which is the definition of K<sub>m</sub>.
(c) 95 % of V<sub>max</sub> needs S = 19 K<sub>m</sub> = 19 × 25 = 475 mmol/L, far above any blood value.
(d) The ratio of actual to straight-line rate is K<sub>m</sub>/(K<sub>m</sub> + S). For K<sub>m</sub> = 25: 25/45 = 0.56, so the response at 20 mmol/L is 44 % below the straight line.
For apparent K<sub>m</sub> = 60: 60/80 = 0.75, only 25 % below. Raising the apparent K<sub>m</sub> straightens the response over 0–20 mmol/L, at the cost of a smaller signal.
examples.answer: (a) 20.0 µmol min⁻¹ mg⁻¹; (b) 60.0 = V<sub>max</sub>/2; (c) 475 mmol/L; (d) 56 % of the straight-line rate with K<sub>m</sub> 25 mmol/L, 75 % with apparent K<sub>m</sub> 60 mmol/L.

examples.question: An antibody on a sensor has K<sub>d</sub> = 1.0 nmol/L for its antigen. Find the fraction of sites occupied at antigen concentrations of 0.10, 1.0 and 9.0 nmol/L, and say what this means for the measuring range.
steps: Going from 1.0 to 9.0 nmol/L, a ninefold rise, only moves θ from 0.50 to 0.90; the signal changes little above a few times K<sub>d</sub>.
examples.answer: θ = 0.091, 0.50 and 0.90. The useful range is roughly 0.1 to 10 times K<sub>d</sub>, here about 0.1–10 nmol/L; a tighter antibody (smaller K<sub>d</sub>) moves the range lower.

traps: An antibody is not a catalyst: it binds without turnover, so V<sub>max</sub> and K<sub>m</sub> do not apply to it.
K<sub>m</sub> is a concentration in mmol/L, not a rate; the rate units belong to V<sub>max</sub>.
Smaller Kd means tighter binding; a large Kd is the weak antibody.
The K<sub>m</sub> measured in free solution is not the apparent K<sub>m</sub> of the immobilised layer.

quiz.a: 1 U = 1 µmol of substrate converted per minute.

quiz.q: Why does an antibody not obey Michaelis–Menten kinetics?
quiz.a: It binds without turnover; there is no catalytic cycle, so V<sub>max</sub> and K<sub>m</sub> do not apply.

quiz.q: V<sub>max</sub> = 80 µmol min⁻¹ mg⁻¹, K<sub>m</sub> = 4.0 mmol/L. Find v at S = 12 mmol/L.
An immobilised enzyme shows apparent K<sub>m</sub> of 20 mmol/L against 5 mmol/L in solution. Give two reasons.
quiz.a: Substrate must diffuse through the layer; crowding and wrong orientation reduce accessible active sites.

quiz.q: Which is tighter binding, Kd = 1 nM or Kd = 10 µM?
A 20-mer probe has high G+C. What happens to Tm and to stringency?
quiz.a: Tm rises; hybridisation is stronger, so the wash must be hotter or lower in salt to keep specificity.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry uses lateral-flow antibody tests, aptamers as synthetic recognition elements, CRISPR-based nucleic acid tests and molecularly imprinted polymers. Surface crowding and Debye-length screening decide whether a label-free antibody sensor works in undiluted serum. Search 'aptamer biosensor', 'lateral flow immunoassay' and 'Debye length screening' next.
